en: The *Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa*:

With the luster of conch-shells, milk, lotus stalks, white water-lilies, and radiant pearl necklaces; with surfaces darkened by clouds of incense from golden *agaru* wood; and bearing fluttering banners.
I pay homage to that Sage, whose feet are not brushed by the crowns of gods, nāgas, and yakṣas, and who is adorned by excellent, praiseworthy elements resembling mountains.
"May the True Dharma triumph!
thus said the nun Śrutasomā.
"There exists karma that leads to a short lifespan."
There is karma that leads to a short lifespan; thus, the destinies of karma have been analyzed in detail according to their proper order.
There are ten advantages to the life of a forest-dwelling mendicant, and there are ten grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).
All the strands of sensual pleasure are joined according to their proper order.
There are ten benefits for those who perform the act of joining the palms in homage at a Tathāgata’s shrine with incense, flowers, and parasols. What are the ten benefits?

But has not the Blessed One stated in the *Ekottarika-āgama*—in detail: "O monks, however many beings there may be—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost among those beings, namely, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One"?
And a verse was also spoken:
Thus the Buddha is inconceivable, and the Buddha-dharma is also inconceivable;
if the Dharma is indeed inconceivable, the Buddha too is inconceivable,
and for one who has inconceivable faith, the maturation [of that faith] is also inconceivable.
How are there ten qualities of the flower-parasols and so forth? It is said:
it is exactly as stated in the sūtra;
it is precisely thus and not otherwise.
Those who have faith in the Buddha, and likewise in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and who have practiced accordingly.
The ripening of their inconceivable faith is also inconceivable;
however, as for those whose minds are impaired by false views, they ask: "How can there be any fruit from what is given to a stūpa of a Buddha who has entered final nirvāṇa?"
Because there is no recipient,
for those who hold such perverted views,
the Blessed One said: "There are these ten benefits of the parasols and other offerings."
By means of this very happiness, let them perform meritorious deeds;
that will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
Moreover, all these virtues are said to be included within these very [virtues].
But how is it that faith placed in the Blessed One is inconceivable? It is said:
as it is stated here in this very *Karmavibhaṅga*, so it is in other sūtras as well.
Nevertheless, for the sake of those of dull intellect, this repetition is made;
as in the case of the elders Karṇa, Īsumana, and others:
"By the gift of a single flower, [one dwells in heaven] for eighty koṭis of kalpas."
This is difficult to believe;
such is the inconceivable nature of karmic fruition.
Likewise, through the gift of a handful of dust, Aśoka and others attained the sovereignty of a universal monarch and the fruit of stream-entry.
This is inconceivable and difficult to believe.

For instance, by offering a single alms-meal to Aniruddha and others, [the donor] attained the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), the seven kingdoms of the gods, and finally, in his last existence, the state of an Arhat.
Many such examples could be cited.
Moreover, by means of a single inconceivable [act], one pervades everything.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Abhidharma-bālakāṇḍa-sūtra*: "The maturation of a single moment of serene faith has been described."

"Ānanda, if as a result of a single moment of serene faith while wandering in saṃsāra, one exercises sovereignty seven times among the gods who wield power over the creations of others (paranirmitavaśavartin),
and seven times among those who delight in their own creations (nirmāṇarati),"
Seven times among the gods of the Heaven of Joy (*Sukhita*),
and seven times having been born among the Yāma gods, he exercises sovereignty;
he exercises thirty-six reigns as Indra.
He exercises sovereignty over the seventy-two thousand Mahārājika gods;
he exercises sovereignty over millions upon millions of universal monarchies (cakravarti-rājyas).
If it were not for sovereignty, this would still be the fruit of a single moment of serene faith.
Moreover, it is said that even a Śrāvaka can become a Buddha;
for example, Buddhahood was attained by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara through the offering of a garland of lamps.
This too would be unbelievable to those who lack faith.
Regarding such deeds as these,
which people in the world do not have faith in,
the Blessed One said to those who lack faith and possess inferior inclinations: "There are these ten virtues of bowing to a caitya."
This is the detailed explanation.
As for the greatness of the Buddhas who are perfect in qualities, it is not mentioned only in the *Agatāsūtra*;
it is also stated in the *Brāhmaṇasūtra*: "I am indeed the foremost, the best of brahmins in the world."
Thus the Sūtra is to be applied:
for example, the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the great seer Koṭu and the ascetic Śela for the sake of their discipline,
and he was invited by them to a meal.
And having understood this from them, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance: "The Vedas have the fire-sacrifice as their mouth; the Gāyatrī is the mouth of the meters;
the king is the mouth of men; the ocean is the mouth of rivers."
The sun is the foremost of the stars; fire is the foremost of things that burn;
the Perfectly Awakened One is the foremost of those who aspire to merit and strive with diligence.
The Blessed One demonstrates this:
just as among all sacrifices being performed, the Agnihotra is the foremost;
and among the Vedas, the Gāyatrī is the foremost.
The king is the foremost of all men;
the ocean is the best of rivers;
the moon is the preeminent among the stars.

Just as the sun is the foremost of all that give heat, illuminating thousands of world-systems, so too is he who thinks, "What is given to this one person yields great fruit. The Blessed One said: "The Perfectly Awakened One is the foremost among those worthy of offerings."
For this reason as well, the Blessed One is supreme.
This sūtra should also be understood in detail from the *Brāhmaṇa-nipāta* in the Āgama.

And as it was said by the Blessed One in the *Dakṣiṇāvibhaṅga-sūtra*: "Ānanda, among those worthy of offerings who are individuals, this is the foremost: namely, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One."
Thus should the supremacy of the Blessed One be declared:
just as in the *Mahāsamājīya* and other sūtras such as the *Parinirvāṇa*, there was an assembly of gods extending twelve yojanas;
and just as he was honored by the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven and others during the Great Miracle.
Having witnessed the Great Miracle, many hundreds of non-Buddhist teachers went forth;
likewise, the ascetics headed by Uruvilvākāśyapa went forth,
as did the wandering mendicants headed by Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
And the Brahmins, such as Vasiṣṭha, Bhāradvāja, and others who were lying in the Brahmāyu [bed], were filled with faith;
likewise, kings such as Prasenajit and Bimbisāra.
The householders, such as Anāthapiṇḍada, Ghoṣila, and others—
likewise those among the gods who are foremost and those among humans—
have placed their faith in the Blessed One.
For this reason also, the Blessed One is supreme.
Moreover, as it is said in the *Ekottarikāgratā-sūtra*: "Endowed with the foremost dharma, having become the foremost among gods and humans, he has attained [it] and is filled with joy.
By this it is meant that the dharma leading to nirvāṇa has been realized.
For that reason, he is the foremost.
What is the reason? Even when he was previously a bodhisattva, the gods approached him, as described in the *Govinda-sūtra*.
In the *Śatavarga* and the *Tāpasa-sūtra*, Indra approached [the Buddha] and asked:
"Was he not then endowed with the supreme dharmas (*agra-dharma*), and has he now realized the path leading to Nirvana?"
Therefore it is supreme.
Even though the dharmas have been taught in this way, some say: (KVU, Vaidya 214)

The Buddha has attained final nirvāṇa and reached liberation. When it is said that the Buddha has indeed passed into final nirvāṇa, who receives the incense, flowers, and so forth that are offered to his stūpa or his image?
Those who do not know the established tenets of the Buddha’s teaching will find this statement unbelievable, or even more wicked than what has preceded it.
This very Dharma which is being taught by the Blessed One is the body of the Blessed One,
and it stands even now.
When he has disappeared, the Buddha will have entered parinirvāṇa.
As long as the Dharma remains, the Buddha does not enter parinirvāṇa.
What is the reason for this?

The body of the Blessed One is the Dharma-body, which is his ultimate body. When, by means of that Dharma being taught, one attains the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning, [that is the Dharma-body].
The fruit of non-returning and the state of arhatship;
for this purpose we have gone forth, as a means to attain the fruits.
The Buddha remains; fruits will be attained.
He has not entered final nirvana. In that case, this fault would arise.
"But for us, the fruits will still be obtained even today; he has not yet entered final nirvāṇa. In that case, this fault would arise."
But even now, fruits are still being obtained by us.
For those who have initiated vigor, nothing is difficult to accomplish.
While the Buddha remains present, all this that ought to be done is performed.
For this reason as well, it should be known that the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body.
As it is said in the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra: "Ānanda, it might occur to you that the Blessed One has entered final nirvāṇa, and that from this day forward there is no Teacher."
It should not be viewed in this way.
From this day forward, Ānanda, the sūtra is your teacher.
In this manner, the Blessed One bestowed the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya.
And from this day forward, he is a Buddha;
the Blessed One demonstrates this.
Likewise, no purpose whatsoever is served by this body born of mother and father;
this he demonstrates when he says: "When I was dwelling in my home..."
At that time, no dharma was fully realized by me;
therefore, the body of a Buddha does not arise from parents.
However, when I departed from my home at twenty-nine years of age,
Those who desire the Dharma through suffering have been amazed by the practice of austerities;
yet no one has ever attained the Dharma through suffering for me,
as it is stated in the *Romaharṣaṇīya-sūtra*.
They should be understood in this way:
for six years he performed difficult austerities, yet by that he did not realize any dharma whatsoever.

Afterwards, having eaten my meal and regained physical strength, I sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the fifteenth day of the full moon in the month of Vaiśākha and attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having gone to Vārāṇasī, I set the Wheel of Dharma in motion;
by means of that Dharma, the realization of the fruits [of the path] is accomplished.
And it is said:
"For this reason also, the Tathāgatas are the Dharmakāya," as the text reads in the Vinaya.
The Blessed One’s maternal aunt said to the Blessed One: "May you live long, O Blessed One!
Regarding that which was said by the Blessed One—'I am not to be addressed as "Gautamī" as before'—how then, Blessed One, am I to be addressed?"
The Blessed One said: "It should be spoken thus: 'May the Dharma of the Blessed One endure for a long time!
This demonstrates that there is no finality for me in this body born of my mother and father.
Therefore, may my body of Dharma remain for a long night; all the thousands of difficult deeds performed by me in saṃsāra were done solely for the sake of the Dharma.
For this reason also, that which is the body of the Blessed One—
[it is] stated in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: "Ānanda, the gods have arrived,
having taken divine sandalwood powders."
And divine *māndārava* flowers,

divine [incense], and so forth— Ānanda, it is in this way that the Tathāgata is honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped. Furthermore, Ānanda, whoever dwells heedfully within my teaching, [he too honors me].
He performs and upholds the Dharma;
by that, I am honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped.
This is what he demonstrates.
The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen of the perfectly awakened Kāśyapa performed the worship of his physical remains.
The Dharma was not upheld;
until the Dharma had disappeared, even while it was being replenished in this way—he acted thus... (he removed).
It should be accumulated.
This is my body;
this he demonstrates—(KVU, Vaidya 215).
"What should be done after I have entered parinirvāṇa?
It has been said that you shall indeed honor the Dharma;
for Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body."
At the time of the Great Parinirvāṇa, the noble Ānanda asked: "How should we perform the rites for the body of the Blessed One once the Blessed One has entered parinirvāṇa?
The Blessed One said: "You should remain free from anxiety;
as for the body, the lay devotees will know what to do."
They will act accordingly. This shows that this very Dharma-body must be protected by you.
"The lay followers are very preoccupied and are unable to uphold the Dharma.
By means of this [text] remaining for a long time, I too shall remain for a long time."

And as it is told in the *Devāvatāra-sūtra*, when the Blessed One descended from the world of the gods, the nun Utpalavarṇā manifested the form of a universal monarch and was the first to pay him homage;
she was delighted,
thinking, "I have paid homage to the Blessed One first."
And having understood that she had attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), he showed this:
"I am not being honored by means of this body born of mother and father which has been described;
rather, I am honored by him by whom the fruit was attained."
And for this very purpose, the verses there state: "The attainment of human birth, the going to the heavenly realms,
and sovereignty over the earth— yet the fruit of stream-entry is supreme."
For this reason as well, the Dharma alone is the body of the Blessed One.
As it is said in the *Bodhimūla-sūtra*: "The Blessed One was dwelling in Ayodhyā.
Now, in the western regions, there lived two monks who were friends."
The two set out to behold the Blessed One;
they entered a great forest,
and being afflicted by thirst, they found water.
One drank it while thirsty.
The second said, "I shall not transgress the Blessed One's training;
this water contains living beings and has not been strained."
The Dharma is the body of the Blessed One;
by protecting it, I have seen the Blessed One in person.
Afflicted by thirst, he paid homage to the Blessed One and passed away.
With a serene mind, he was reborn among the gods.
As for the second monk, having drunk water that was measured out, he proceeded by stages and reached the presence of the Blessed One after many days;
yet that monk who had been reborn among the gods arrived first.

To that monk who had drunk water containing living beings, the Blessed One showed his own body as it was when he was with his parents, saying, "Behold this body of mine. Then, to the monk who had been reborn in the world of the gods, the Blessed One said, "Show your body. Thereupon, he displayed his divine body as a son of the gods.
That monk, filled with agitation, asked: "Blessed One, what is this?
The Blessed One said: "This son of the gods, afflicted by thirst, did not drink water containing living beings;
he has observed the training as prescribed by me."
This second body born of parents was desirous of seeing [me]; having drunk the water along with the vessel, I showed him this body born of parents, saying: "Behold this body;
if no quality whatsoever has been seen by him, then let him behold this body born of parents."
He was not seen by him. For this very reason, the verse was spoken:
"If they step along, foot by foot, leaning on the corner of their robe..."
Those who remain in transgression do not stand in the presence of the Buddha.
Those who, having heard this well-spoken word, practice its meaning even from thousands of yojanas away, they indeed remain in the presence of the Buddha.
And just as the Blessed One approached Nandaka for the sake of his love for the Dharma in order to hear the teaching of the Dharma from him;
and just as it is said in the *Upasthāpanaka-sūtra*: "Search, monks!
He attends upon me and will uphold my Dharma."
Seek out him who upholds my ninefold teaching: the Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Itivṛtta, Gāthā, Udāna, and so forth.
Do not seek one who can provide a body produced from a mother and father.
What is the reason?

As it was said in the *Ṛddhipāda-nipāta* regarding the palace of Mṛgāramātā: "Monks, when the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) have been thus cultivated, the Tathāgata could remain for an eon (*kalpa*) or for the remainder of an eon. This demonstrates: "You are not capable of sustaining my body for an eon;
however, this Dharma must be sustained."
This is my body.
And as it is said in the Mahādeva-sūtra: "May you not be my last [disciples]...
[namely], this Kauṇḍinya."
Among those of great wisdom, Sāriputra is foremost; among those possessed of supernatural powers, Maudgalyāyana;
and among those worthy of offerings, the noble son Subhūti.
In this way, the entire sūtra should be stated;
it is spoken in the *Bhikṣuṇī-agratā-sūtra*, and likewise it is spoken in the *Upāsaka-agratā-sūtra* and the *Upāsikā-agratā-sūtra*.
Likewise, the *Catuṣpariṣatsūtra* states: "O monks, he is distinct, disciplined, confident, and learned."
A preacher of the Dharma who has realized the meaning of the Dharma beautifies the Saṅgha;
[so too does] a bhikṣuṇī.
Lay follower (upāsaka), lay follower (upāsikā), and monks (bhikṣu).
Those who are clear-minded, disciplined, confident, learned, righteous, and established in the meaning of the Dharma adorn the Saṅgha;
that sūtra, too, should be recited.
Moreover:
Even for a single person who has become free from passion, our gift is immeasurable.
As it is said in the Ugra-sūtra: "Behold, O Ugra, when a monk, clothed in his robe, enters and abides in an immeasurable concentration, the overflow of merit from that is immeasurable."
The outflow of the wholesome is the nourishment of happiness.
Thus, having consumed alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick, one dwells having attained immeasurable concentration.
Householder Ugra, it is just as when many great rivers come together into a single unity.
It is not possible for you to calculate that water;
nevertheless, it is reckoned as a vast mass of water, immeasurable and incalculable.
Which are the great rivers?
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarayū, Āryavatī, and Mahī—
their waters cannot be fully enumerated;
nevertheless, that immeasurable and incalculable great mass of water is nonetheless reckoned as such.
In the same way, Ugra, behold how a monk, while using his robes, enters and dwells in immeasurable concentration;
likewise, while using alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick, he enters and dwells in immeasurable concentration.
Immeasurable is the outflow of merit from that, the outflow of the wholesome, which is the sustenance of happiness.
In the same way, even when given to a person who possesses moral discipline, a gift from us yields immeasurable fruit;
this applies likewise to gifts of groves and monasteries,
as stated in the Velāma Sūtra.
The details should be understood from the *Dakṣiṇāsūtra*.
Likewise, the maturation of worship performed at the stūpa of the Blessed One who has entered final nirvāṇa is immeasurable.
As it is stated in the *Karmavibhaṅga*: "There are ten benefits of making offerings to a Tathāgata."
What is the reason? Whatever donor there may be, they give a gift either while aspiring for great wealth, or...
Whether contemplating the happiness of heaven or for the sake of liberation—
all of that has been explained, as well as how one comes to possess great enjoyments.
One is reborn in the heavens and swiftly attains parinirvāṇa;
such is the immeasurable ripening of the merit performed at a stūpa.
It is not as with other statements, such as "He seizes Devadatta with this.
There is indeed an action for us: he who steals what has been given to a stūpa incurs immeasurable demerit.
No comparison can be made for them, nor can their measure be determined;
whatever gold, silver, wealth, grain, clothing, ornaments, and so forth belong to all sentient beings upon this circle of the earth—
Whoever commits a theft of any of those things, the sin of one who steals what has been given to a stūpa is far greater than that sin.
This is our established doctrine: that which is given to a stūpa must be applied to the stūpa itself.
Whatever belongs to the Saṃgha must be utilized by the Saṃgha alone;
this is our own established doctrine. Just as our Blessed One remains present, so too [should it be].
And the service rendered toward him yields immeasurable maturation.
But how is it that when one gives to those external deities, what kind of merit bears fruit?
They are understood in this way.
"The Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa;
our deities remain present.
And thus we say: whatever one offers—whether food, incense, flowers, fragrance, lamps, meals, clothing, ornaments, silver, or gold—to those who remain..."
Or they offer [it]; why does he not take hand from hand?
Now, if he does not take it, [what then?]
What is the specific distinction between the Buddha and them? Now,
if it is thought that the images of those gods are worshipped as their representations,
[we reply] that for us as well, the Dharma-body of the Buddha remains present.
And virtues are honored;
for those who offer incense, fragrance, and flowers to images,
when this is done, merit accrues to us as if it were given to the stūpas themselves.
They are honored;
because he does not accept [offerings], therefore there are no gods.
Now, O gods, if they exist,
why do they not accept [it]?
What is the reason?
The Blessed One has said: "Through the coming together of three factors, a gift becomes of great fruit.
That is to say, there must be a donor;
and there must be the object to be given, such as silver, gold, and so forth."
Those who are worthy of offerings,
whether they be recipients— be they gods or humans—
it is through the coming together of these three factors that [the result arises].
A gift given hand-to-hand, where there is a direct exchange of giving and receiving, does not yield great fruit.
If this were indeed the case,
why would they not accept it?
Of those who are devoted to it;
or, if they accept [it],
of those who are devoted to it.
Now, if they do not accept [the food], having done what?
Is it not reasonable that such anger on the part of the devotees is the cause? Or is it true for them, but not for us, that "the god is angry"?
It is said:
If they are not angry,
for what reason do they not accept [the offerings]?
Therefore, he does not exist;
this is the third reason.
Furthermore, those who are devoted to those gods offer gold or silver at the base of their feet.
"In this way, what bondage could there be for Your Majesty?
[The king replied: "In that case, if it is used for his incense, flowers, perfumes, or for making garlands, then the fruit of merit belongs to the one by whom it was given."
Now, if that substance has been taken by others,
there is no fruit of merit for the donor; and as for those who take it, they say, "We are devotees of the gods, living at the feet of the gods."

"We and the deity are one. For those who have not been granted the sovereignty of the deity, what is the reason for their misappropriation of the deity's property? The property of the deity may be taken by another.
In this case, would a substance be taken from the Lord that is equal to him or superior to him?
And there is no one at all who is equal to the Lord,
much less anyone who is more distinguished.
They are even more distinguished.
For what reason?
Because they perform prostrations before him.
And they sleep at the feet of the King;
since they are more distinguished,
for what purpose is the King being propitiated?

Now, if there were no sin in taking the property of the gods in that case, then there would likewise be no sin for other thieves who live by theft and who seize the property and possessions of others.
For them, too, there is no sin.
Now, if a mother, father, son, king, or servant takes property according to its nature— just as a son takes ancestral property,
or a servant takes the property of a king— [there is no fault].
We too are likewise;
yet even this is incorrect.
What is the reason?
But for a son who takes the property of his father, there is a great sin.
Now, if it is thought that [the father's property] is like the property of a king’s servant,
it is said in reply:
A king would give his own son, let alone a servant, to someone who seizes what has not been given;
therefore, this is the illustration for our sake.
And as for their agreement that "we are devotees of the gods and subsist upon their feet;
therefore, we take [this]," that is improper.
What is the reason?
Because those who are devoted to the gods do not take the property of the gods;
yet, if they were to take it, [they would be guilty].
They do not become devotees of that [deity];
no one who possesses devotion takes the property of the deity;
they have no devotion for the deity.
They have devotion toward the property of the gods;
there is no sin whatsoever found in those who take what has not been given.
What is the reason?
Because the ancient seers have said that when the root is severed, for one whose affection for his father has vanished from the branch of the tree of asceticism, all other people [are likewise lost].
This is what is meant: he who takes the property of the gods which has not been given [is such a person].
There is nothing whatsoever that he must not do.
For what reason?
Because they are not possessed of devotion.
Now, those who are devoted—what enemies have been proclaimed to Your Majesty?
Or if it is thought: "Just as they are free from the sense of 'mine,' they have no need for his property."
It is said:
there is scriptural tradition (*śruti*) among certain gods that the destruction of the sacrifice to the gods and the seizure of the earth were committed [by them].
Why, then, are they not considered "mine"?
[The opponent asks: "Was this given by us alone, and not by the deity? [The author] replies: "For what purpose was it given by the donor?"
It was given to us alone;
because it was relinquished to the King,
therefore it was not given to you.
Now, it might be thought: "It is simply the pleasure of the Lord that we receive [these things].
For what purpose did the Lord not state that he is the giver, saying: 'Give these to them;
once given to them, I shall exist'?"
Since no donor was mentioned by the King,
and it was taken by them, therefore there is no fruit of merit for the donor.
And for those who take [it], there is the taking of what was not given. Now, if it is thought that [this applies] to the merit of a deity—[that is] incorrect.
What is the reason?
Because the King himself did not take that object and hand it over from his own hand to theirs.
As the Blessed One has said: "A gift becomes of great fruit through the coming together of three factors. Why, then, was it not given in this manner?
And thus these [beings] are distinguished from the very same [source].
It is said: he will even commit the theft of another's property;
and there are some who live even by various [means].
They do not take that property of others because they lack the power [to do so],
or because some fear the king.
These are the [causes] for the gods, for those devoted to the gods, and for the religious duty toward the gods.
Furthermore, this historical fact must be told here: who would accept even the pilgrimage of Your Majesty to those places?
And who would accept their pilgrimage to the vast banks of those rivers where they have passed away?
Who would accept their pilgrimage to those sacred sites (tīrtha) where they cause [the Dharma] to be heard?

Now, if it is thought: "We shall bathe in the river with reference to a sacred ford (tīrtha); therefore, [the merit] of that river's sacred ford is attained"—then our position is established. For what reason?
The body of our Buddha remains;
his virtues are honored,
and the stupas accept incense and flowers.
— Those rivers, having abandoned their ancient course, flow through this region of the earth;
and those sages have passed away.
Therefore, no one accepts their pilgrimage to the sacred fords.
Such indeed are the honors and other services rendered to the sages, those who are Brahmarṣis. What is the reason?
Because some have attained realization therein.
Its origin is Brahmā;
for some, it is the worship of the Ākāśyapīyas; for others, Īśvara is the creator.
